titleStmt.title: Towards tight Best-and Worst-Case Bounds with Heaviside Real-Time Analysis

analytic.title: Towards tight Best-and Worst-Case Bounds with Heaviside Real-Time Analysis

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In real-time scheduling theory, most of the literature focusses on worst-case response time analysis to predict a deadline violation. The extension of the analysis from singlecore processors to distributed real-time systems also requires the computation of the best-case response time to analyze end-to-end latencies. However, less work is published for bestcase analysis. On top of that, the approaches for best-and worst-case analysis differ, although, intuitively, they should have a symmetry. In this paper, we present for the first time a general response time analysis for fixed-priority schedulings where the best-and worst-case are derived as special cases of a time-based response time analysis. The time-based model enables us to prove the tightness of our bounds. In experiments, we compare a tight best-and worst-case response time analysis to a simulation of response times in the same model for an industrial task set and discuss the probability of the worst-case.

div.head: Keywords
div.p: real-time scheduling theory, real-time analysis, worstcase response time, best-case response time, fixed-priority scheduling

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time analysis, an open problem is to find a general method that predicts deadline violations for any kind of task model and scheduling policy. The problem of deciding whether a task set is feasible (it meets all deadlines) is known to be NP-hard [17], so that the realtime community [4][16] [18][19][21] [28][31] [32] focusses on solving special cases of the feasibility problem. Particularly, certain feasilibity problems are solvable by computationally efficient algorithms based on the response time analysis (RTA) [13][28] and the horizontal distance method [15] [32]. Both compute a lower and upper bound on the best-and worst-case response time (BCRT and WCRT). The key idea is to bound the interference and hence the BCRT and respectively the WCRT from below and above based on properties of the task and scheduler model instead of analyzing an enumerated set of schedules, known as the busy period approach [16] [31].

The trade-off is the overestimation of the bounds, i.e. the predicted BCRT and WCRT may not be reproducible by a simulation [24]. If the analysis computes an upper bound strictly greater than the WCRT, i.e. if the bound is not tight, then the overestimation, which is the ratio of the upper bound to the WCRT, provides a quality measure for the analysis. However, to calculate the overestimation, we have to know the WCRT which is usually the unknown parameter.

An intuitive idea to measure overestimation is to compute the ratio of the upper bound to a Monte-Carlo (MC) simulated [20] interference function τ (t), see Figure 1. Assume that tasks have a jitter on their request and execution times. The blue graphs represent τ (t) that accumulates the interference on some task τ in the interval [0, t) where the request and execution times of interfering task instances are randomized based on their jitter. Time point 0 is the start point and t is the duration of the simulation. The green and red graphs show an lower and upper bound - τ (t) and + τ (t) on τ (t). The overestimation for some t can be defined as the ratio of + τ (t) to the highest value of the simulated τ (t). Similarly, the underestimation is defined. However, if the simulation never generates the bestor worst-case, then such a definition of under-and overestimation is only an approximation. In Figure 1, we can see that τ (t) never intersects the green and red bounds. The reason can be that the bounds are too pessimistic or that it is just unlikely to generate the bestand worst-case. We cannot identify the reason if we do not know the best and worst-case. In this paper, we present a novel and tight BCRT and WCRT analysis of a preemptive fixed-priority (FP) scheduling with first-come first-served (FCFS) as a tiebreaker in the Heaviside real-time analysis (HeRTA) [30]. Contrary to the literature, our analyses are derived from a time-based model of interference from which best-and worst case are derived as special cases by generalizing the busy period to the concept of remaining load [30]. This approach enables us to prove the tightness of our analyses which provides evidence for the existence of schedules that generate the predicted BCRT and WCRT. Furthermore, our analyses are the basis to calculate under-and overestimations of other analyses that trade-off precision for computational complexity. On top of that, our analyses can be applied to investigate the likelyhood of best-and worst-case since we know that the distance between the tight bounds and the simulation as in Figure 1 must occur due to unlikely events. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related work. Section 3 presents our model and Section 4 our analysis followed by experiments in Section 5. Finally, Section 6 presents our conclusions.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Two well-studied models for bounding the interference for BCRT and WCRT analysis are the real-time calculus (RTC) and SymTA/S [28][32]. Both have different overestimations since they have different assumptions. The models are compared in empirical studies [14][24] and also formally [25]. However, their different overestimations cannot be explained. One reason is that the overestimation in each of the models is not well understood. Both models bound instead of compute the interference function which results in WCRT estimates that cannot always be associated with a simulated response time. Furthermore, analysis results cannot be checked by a simulation due to a missing model of interference as a function of time.

In contrast to the WCRT, the BCRT is only discussed for certain task models. The BCRT analysis is motivated by the analysis of end-to-end latencies [3][33]. Initially, the BCRT is assumed to be 0 [3][33] which is a trival lower bound. Reference [22] presents a lower bound on the BCRT by assuming that all higher-priority tasks exactly finish at the request time of the task under analysis. Reference [10] remove this assumption of [22], by abstracting from offsets. Reference [27] improves the bound to be tight by assuming constrained deadlines.

Reference [11] and [26] provide a BCRT analysis for tasks with jitter and variable execution times, however, they do not model offsets. Reference [5] generalizes the previous approaches to arbitrary deadlines, offsets and jitter, however, assuming the jitter to not be greater than the period. The tightness of bounds is discussed in the RTC [34] for WCRT, however, not for BCRT analysis, wheras [27] shows the tightness of the BCRT analysis for constrained deadlines.

In contrast to the literature which bounds the interference based on busy periods, HeRTA [6][7] [8][30] models interference as a function of time based on the more general concept of remaining load. Hence, HeRTA provides tight BCRTs and WCRTs for hierarchical schedulers without jitter by computing them as the minimum and maximum of all response times in the hyperperiod.

The goal of our work is to extend HeRTA to consider jitter for arbitrary task models and hierarchical schedulers while keeping the tight BCRT and WCRT bounds of HeRTA. This paper is the first step towards that goal. More precisely, we allow interfering tasks to jitter, while the task under analysis does not jitter.

Our task model allows tasks to have a jitter that is greater than the period. Hence, a job ι m,n+1 may be requested before ι m,n and interfere with ι m,n . To avoid such interference, we apply FCFS as a tie-breaker, that schedules the jobs of the same task by their request times without jitter. This showcases the idea that we can control the scheduling of the jobs without restricting our task model to e.g. jitter smaller than period. More formally, the scheduler ι,mn returns 1, if ι mn interferes with the JUC ι under FP with FCFS tie-breaking, else it returns 0. By multiplying ι,mn to the Heaviside mask (A mn , Δ b a ), we model the interference Γ,ι (Δ b a ) under FP in the interval [a, b), as the product1 in (5) only returns c mn , if ι,mn = 1 and (A mn , Δ b a ) = 1. Note that the interference function Γ,ι (Δ b a ) considers for each job ι mn whether it interferes with ι in [a, b). This job-based computation of interference enables the proof of tight bounds since we can argue for each job separately whether it causes interference under best-and worst-case assumptions.

HeRTA computes the response time of the JUC as the sum of the remaining load and the interference on the JUC as a function of time instead of bounding the response time using busy periods. In contrast to the busy period approaches [5][23] [28], HeRTA does not assume the bestand worst-case to be known. The idea of HeRTA is to apply a response time analysis, shown in Theorem 2, to all jobs in the hyperperiod of the task under analysis, so that the BCRT and WCRT of the task are the minimum and maximum of these response times, respectively.

div.p: By Theorem 3 and 4, we can now compute tight lower and upper response time bounds, i.e. the BCRT and WCRT for the given task model. More precisely, task parameters have no limitations except for the assumption that the JUC itself has no jitter. This is a first step towards a tight BCRT and WCRT analysis for a general task model and arbitrary hierarchical schedulers. The computational complexity of our analysis can be reduced by transforming Heaviside to ceiling and floor functions using Table 1 of [30]. Using ( 15) and ( 16), an RTA for a task can be formulated considering all jobs in a hyperperiod with a similar complexity to [2].

div.head: Experimental Evaluation
div.p: This paper is the first one to compare a tight BCRT and WCRT bound to simulated response times where both, bounded and simulated response time, are computed in the same model. More formally, we investigate the factors by which the tight upper and lower bound on the response time of Theorem 3 differ from MC simulated response times using Theorem 2. The idea is that the ratio between the WCRT bound and the maximum of the simulated response times is an indicator for the probability of generating the worst-case since we know by Theorem 4 that the WCRT bound is tight. Hence, such a ratio does not represent overestimation. Instead, we expect that the ratio should indicate the probability of the worst-case.

To measure the ratio, Theorem 2 is applied to randomly generated job sequences of a task set, i.e. the request and execution times of jobs are randomly selected from the request and execution time interval. If we generate multiple randomized schedules of a given task set in which the same JUC occurs, we can compute its response times in all schedules using Theorem 2 and therefore get an empirical minimum and maximum response time that can be compared to the bounds of Theorem 3. Our expectations are that the ratios depend on the range of the jitter of each task and also on the request time of the JUC, since, it is known that the worst-case may not occur at time point zero when tasks have offsets [2]. Hence, we investigate the ratio of the bounds to the simulated response times as a function of jitter and offset. Experimental Setup.
We investigate a simplified industrial task set from our project partner [12]:

The JUC in the task set Γ 1 is ι 5,0 . We compute the ratio of the WCRT r + 5,0 of the JUC ι 5,0 to the maximum of the simulated response times r + 5,0 of the JUC. Similarly, we compute the ratio of the minimum simulated response time r - 5,0 to the BCRT r - 5,0 of the JUC. These ratios are computed for three different offsets φ 5 ∈ {1500, 8100, 14700} of task τ 5 to analyze the JUC at three equidistant time points in the period of p 5 = 20000. Hence, we get three experiments where the JUC has the request time A ∈ {1500, 8100, 14700}. For each A ∈ {1500, 8100, 14700}, we also consider three jitter scaling factors ρ ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5} that determine the jitter of each interfering task of τ 5 as follows:

By combining the three values of ρ and of φ 5 , we get nine task sets in total in which we compare the bounds and the simulated response times with respect to jitter of interfering tasks and the request time of the JUC. Experimental Procedure. For each of the nine task sets, we generate 3000 MC simulations where the response time of the JUC is computed based on randomly generated job sequences. All random choices are made using a uniform distribution. In each simulation, the request time and execution time of an interfering job are randomly chosen based on the jitter interval [ j - m , j + m ] and the execution time interval [c - m , c + m ] of the task τ m . The request time of the JUC is equal to φ 5 of the given experiment. The execution time of the JUC is randomly chosen in the execution time interval of τ 5 . After generating a random job sequence, the response time of the JUC is computed using the RTA of Theorem 2. After computing the 3000 response times of the JUC, we calculate the minimum and maximum simulated response time of the JUC that are denoted by r - 5,0 and r + 5,0 . Then, the BCRT r - 5,0 and WCRT r + 5,0 of the JUC are computed. Afterwards, the ratios r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 and r - 5,0 /r - 5,0 are calculated. r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 describes that factor of the tight WCRT bound to the maximum simulated response time. r - 5,0 /r - 5,0 calculates the factor of the minimum simulated response time to the tight BCRT bound. Experimental Results. The results of the experiment are shown in Table 1. Each row describes one of the nine setups of the request time A of the JUC and the jitter scaling factor ρ. We can see that for a fixed A 5,0 and increasing ρ the tight WCRT bound r + 5,0 increases as a 1 Ratios and bounds of the response time of ι 5,0 .

higher jitter means a higher probability that the busy period and request time interval of the JUC and the interfering job intersect, hence, increasing the response time of the JUC. Inversely, the tight BCRT bound decreases for increasing jitter since the chance of that intersection becomes smaller.

If we consider a constant ρ and compare the different A 5,0 , then we cannot observe a linear relation between the request time of the JUC and its BCRT or WCRT. For example, if ρ = 0, then the highest r + 5,0 is at A 5,0 = 1500 compared to ρ = 0.5 with the highest reponse time at A 5,0 = 8100. Similarly, one cannot state which request time minimizes the BCRT. Generalizing, the request time of the JUC, or the offset of the task, may not indicate the BCRT or WCRT which is also known from the literature [2]. Considering the ratios in Table 1, we observe for a fixed request time A 5,0 that the change of the ratio r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 from ρ = 0 to ρ = 0.25 is greater than the change from ρ = 0.25 to ρ = 0.5. A reason may be that longer busy periods are more likely with higher jitter, so that the worst-case occurs more often which decreases the ratio r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 . At ρ = 0.25, the busy periods may be long enough for the RTA to predict higher WCRTs while in the average case, such busy periods are rare, leading to a higher ratio r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 . Figure 3 illustrates the smaller increase of r + 5,0 /r + 5,0 when ρ goes from 0.25 to 0.5 as the majority of response times tends to increase. For a fixed request time A 5,0 and increasing ρ, we observe that the separated distributions for ρ = 0 tend to merge to one distribution since more schedules and hence response times are possible with increasing jitter. Furthermore, the mean value tends to shift towards the WCRT. For the best case ratio r - 5,0 / r - 5,0 , we cannot state the inverse behavior, i.e. that higher jitter may imply a higher r - 5,0 / r - 5,0 ratio. A reason may be the specific task parameters of Γ 1 . In future work, we have to extend the experiments to randomized tasksets.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This work presented a BCRT and WCRT analysis for FP scheduling and FCFS as a tie-breaker. The analysis is derived from a time-based RTA based on which we also proved the tightness of our bounds. Hence, our analysis has no under-or overestimation of the BCRT and WCRT. In fact, one can quantify the under-or overestimation of other RTAs based on our tight bounds. Furthermore, the novelty of the presented model is that it provides the basis to quantify the probability of the WCRT due to the common model of the time-based and worst-case RTA. The analysis of this work applies to FP scheduling where all tasks except for the task under analysis have a jitter. In future work, we want to extend our analysis to arbitrary jitter models and hierarchical task schedulers from HeRTA. Moreover, we want to derive further abstractions for best-and worst-case analysis and investigate the trade-off to the computational complexity of busy period approaches.
